metadata.note: This transcript has been prepared from the audio recording. Minor edits have been made for clarity. Substantive content is unchanged.

transcript.speaker: R. Henderson (RSM)
transcript.text: Right, thank you for making the time, Jane. As I mentioned, this is a routine inspection interview. I'd like to go through your AML procedures — how things work day to day, not just what's in the policy document. Shall we start with how a new matter comes in?

transcript.speaker: J. Smith (MLRO)
transcript.text: Of course. So when we take on a new client, the fee earner opens the file and sends out the client care pack — that's the engagement letter, the ID checklist, all of that. We ask for passport or driving licence, proof of address, and we run an electronic ID check through our provider as well.

transcript.speaker: R. Henderson
transcript.text: And the electronic ID — which provider do you use?

transcript.speaker: J. Smith
transcript.text: We use SmartSearch. It runs against multiple databases — credit reference, electoral roll, mortality register. We get a report back with a confidence score and we keep that on the file.

transcript.speaker: R. Henderson
transcript.text: Good. And if the electronic check comes back with a low confidence score or a partial match?

transcript.speaker: J. Smith
transcript.text: Then we'd ask for additional documentary evidence. Maybe a second form of photo ID, or a bank statement to corroborate the address. We wouldn't proceed until we were satisfied. That's happened a few times — usually it's something innocent like a recent house move where the electoral roll hasn't caught up.

transcript.speaker: R. Henderson
transcript.text: That's clear. Let's talk about source of funds. Can you walk me through what happens when you're verifying where the purchase money is coming from?

transcript.speaker: J. Smith
transcript.text: Yes, so we send out the source of funds declaration with the client care pack. The client fills that in — where the money's coming from, how much from each source. Savings, gift, sale of another property, whatever it might be. And then we ask for the bank statements to back it up.

transcript.speaker: R. Henderson
transcript.text: And when the bank statements come in, what does the review process actually look like? Who looks at them and what are they checking for?

transcript.speaker: J. Smith
transcript.text: So the fee earner will have a look at them when they come in. To be honest, it's — we're mainly just checking that the numbers broadly stack up. You know, if someone says they've got six hundred thousand in savings, you'd expect to see that sort of figure sitting in the account. We're not forensic accountants, we're just making sure it looks about right for what they've declared. If it looks consistent, we tick the box on the file checklist and move on. I'll have a glance at the file when I do my review but by that point it's usually all been dealt with.

transcript.speaker: R. Henderson
transcript.text: When you say 'tick the box on the file checklist' — is there a formal sign-off process? A written record of what was checked and by whom?

transcript.speaker: J. Smith
transcript.text: There's the checklist, which has a column for initials and date. So yes, whoever reviewed it signs it off. But in terms of a detailed written assessment of the source of funds — no, we don't do a separate write-up for every file. It would be quite onerous given our volume. The checklist is our record that it's been looked at.

transcript.speaker: R. Henderson
transcript.text: And for higher-value transactions, or overseas clients — does the process change at all?

transcript.speaker: J. Smith
transcript.text: In principle it should, yes. We'd want more bank statement coverage and we might ask more questions. But the actual review process is much the same — you're still looking at the statements and checking they're consistent with the declaration. I'd probably have a closer look at those ones myself rather than just relying on the fee earner.

transcript.speaker: R. Henderson
transcript.text: OK. And if you saw something unusual on a bank statement — a large unexplained deposit, for instance — what would happen?

transcript.speaker: J. Smith
transcript.text: We'd ask the client about it. Get an explanation. If we weren't happy with the explanation then I'd consider whether we need to make a report. But nine times out of ten there's a perfectly reasonable explanation — bonus payment, tax refund, that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: R. Henderson
transcript.text: Let's move on to the nominated officer role. You're the MLRO here — can you tell me about the internal reporting process?

transcript.speaker: J. Smith
transcript.text: Yes, so if anyone in the firm has a concern, they fill in the internal suspicion report form and submit it to me. I review it, decide whether we need to make a SAR to the NCA, and I record my decision either way. We've got the forms in the procedures manual and everyone knows the process — we cover it in the annual training.

transcript.speaker: R. Henderson
transcript.text: When was the last internal report you received?

transcript.speaker: J. Smith
transcript.text: I'd have to check the log. I think it was about four months ago — it turned out to be nothing, but the fee earner was right to flag it. I was pleased they did, actually.

transcript.speaker: R. Henderson
transcript.text: Good. And the training — you mentioned annual training. When did staff last receive AML training?

transcript.speaker: J. Smith
transcript.text: We did a session in... it would have been March this year. Whole team, couple of hours. We went through the recent changes, the source of wealth compliance notice, red flags, that sort of thing. I've got the training record with the signatures if you'd like to see it.

transcript.speaker: R. Henderson
transcript.text: Yes, I'll take a look at that. Just coming back to one thing — you mentioned that for source of funds, the review is primarily checking that figures look consistent with the declaration. Your written procedure refers to making 'reasonable enquiries' and retaining copies of 'all relevant documentation'. How do you reconcile the two?

transcript.speaker: J. Smith
transcript.text: I think... well, we do retain the copies. Everything goes on the file — the declaration, the bank statements, all of it. The enquiry part is the review itself. We're looking at the documents, we're making sure they're consistent. I take your point that we could probably document the actual assessment more formally, but the substance of the check is happening, it's just perhaps not being recorded in as much detail as it could be.

transcript.speaker: R. Henderson
transcript.text: Thank you, Jane. Let's move on to your risk assessment procedures...

truncation_note: Interview continues — remaining topics: risk assessment procedures, ongoing monitoring, file review processes, sanctions screening. Full transcript available on request.
